claims.text: A thin amorphous metallic-glass interlayer decreases interface coherency in HEA multilayers.
The amorphous interlayer promotes dislocation nucleation.
Introducing the amorphous interlayer enables a controlled transition from diffusion-mediated creep to dislocation-mediated creep.
The initial HEA multilayers have fully coherent crystalline interfaces.
Creep behavior in the relevant high-temperature and high-stress regime is sensitive to interface structure.
The amorphous interlayer acts as a dislocation-nucleation site.
The amorphous layer lowers coherency strain at the interface.
The amorphous layer disrupts continuous lattice matching across the interface.
The amorphous layer restrains atomic diffusion paths.
Increasing temperature and stress causes the interlayer-containing system to shift toward creep involving dislocation motion.
Under identical test conditions, interlayer-containing HEA multilayers have a greater contribution from dislocation-mediated creep than fully coherent HEA multilayers.
The proposed creep-mechanism transition produces a change in creep rate.
The proposed creep-mechanism transition produces a change in dislocation density.
HEA multilayers with fully coherent crystalline interfaces primarily exhibit diffusion-mediated creep under similar conditions.
The transitional effect occurs only within an optimal range of interlayer thickness and composition.
An excessively thick amorphous interlayer may cause other mechanical instabilities.
An excessively thin amorphous interlayer may not sufficiently disrupt interface coherency.
